newsitem.title: USA: Neptune to acquire APL shipping for $825 million.
newsitem.headline: Neptune to acquire APL shipping for $825 million.

text.p: Singaporean shipping firm Neptune Orient Lines LTD said on Sunday it agreed to buy container carrier APL Ltd in a transaction valued at about $825 million.
Neptune said it will pay $33.50 per share for all 24.6 million outstanding shares of APL, which will become a wholly owned subsidiary of Neptune Orient.
The boards of each company have unanimously approved the transaction, which comes during a time of rapid industry consolidation and rate pressure.
Neptune said APL will retain its name and will continue its transportation operations, headed by its existing management in Oakland, Calif.

In a statement, Lua Cheng Eng, deputy chairman and chief executive of Neptune Orient, said both companies expect to realize cost savings of at least $130 million a year from the consolidation of certain operations and improved efficiencies, including lowered inland costs and reduced terminal expenses.
Neptune Orient said the merged entity's combined revenues would exceed $4 billion, making it one of the largest shipping companies in the world.
The firms will operate a total fleet of 113 vessels, including 76 container ships with a total of about 200,000 TEUs (twenty-foot equivalent units) vessel capacity.
NOL employs about 4,800 people worldwide, while Oakland, Calif.-based APL has about 4,000 employees.
In an interview with Reuters, Lua Cheng Eng was asked about potential employee cutbacks. "We have no specific details on this particular point and would not want to speculate on the number," he said.

The cost efficiencies will come mainly from NOL's ability in the United States to utilize APL's extremely sophisticated container terminals and stack-trains and APL's access to NOL's strong marketing capacity in Asia.
Lim How Teck, deputy chief excutive officer of NOL, said he expects there will be a period of 18 to 24 months before the companies will see the full effect of cost efficiencies.
"We should see accretion to earnings at that point," he said.
In January, APL said it expected rate pressures to continue through 1997 after the company experienced rate reductions in all of its markets during the previous year.
APL said the pressure would continue due to excess capacity and slow market growth, particularly in the first half of the year.

In February, APL and other members of the Transpacific Stablization Agreement, a major shipping conference, announced plans to raise rates on Asian imports to the United States following significant declines in freight rates during 1996 on trade from Asia.
The conference, which controls a majority of the $200 billion Asia-to-United States trade, plans to initiate the increase in May.
Both carriers are currently members of the conference and are participating in the rate hike.
